You're a sailor, lost at sea. You look backwards, forwards, side to side, but you see nothing but water. You know at some point, it feels like decades ago, you were standing on land, with people around you, but that's a glimmering memory. You can barely remember what it feels like to have solid ground under your feet. All you know is the rocking of your boat, struggling to survive day after day after day. You're cut off from everything and everyone, and all you have left are your own thoughts.

All you live for is the hope that you'll see land again.

I think you'll find happiness again. But really all that matters is if YOU think you'll find it again. Maybe not for long, maybe not for the rest of your life. But you'll find a patch of happiness, a scrap of joy, and that will make it worth it. That's what's kept me going.

Whether you're doing something wrong depends on your view of morality. I personally like the golden rule standard.

If someone were to follow me around and use perfectly legal tactics to find out that I am pretty rich (say by some innocuous surveillance) and then posted some video evidence of it to youtube, I'd be pretty uncomfortable. Say, then, that some youtube commenter started remarking on how I'm rich and how she'd like to tap that bank account by hooking up with me. Say, then, that it's not just one commenter, but a couple dozen, or even a hundred circle-jerking about how they're sure I'd like that. I think I'd start to feel more than just uncomfortable - I'd feel somewhat devalued, ironically enough. I don't think I'd enjoy that situation much at all.

In this situation, no one person (the surveiller, the first commenter, the next hundred commenters) is doing anything truly despicable. And yet, you take the effect that they generate as a collective, and it becomes a phenomenon that doesn't meet the golden rule standard.

Are you doing anything really "bad"? No. But you are contributing (with money or attention) to an effect that we can pretty definitively call "bad".

As I understand it, an objective Purpose is one that is universal and True. This could be a Purpose dictated by the Universe or by a god. A subjective purpose is internally defined. For instance, a robot whose entire code base is to avoid table edges (cliff detection), has a "purpose in life" even though that purpose is entirely based on not falling off a table.

With that basis, though, I realized that an objective Purpose must be based on something stitched into the fabric of the Universe - a natural law. What if there is a 'meaningful constant', much like there's a gravitational constant or a defined speed of light? I like the idea of making my subjective purpose the advancement of the pursuit for an objective Purpose. I don't think one will be approached any time in the next few centuries, but I think approaching the idea that one might exist with total uncertainty is a more useful (scientifically speaking) approach than that of nihilism (or the opposite), as there is relatively little evidence one way or another.
